Can the minister advise the house when he expects to announce the reduction in the spending estimates for 1967-68 which he has said he intends to make?

Mr. Speaker, I will be making a statement both about the spending in this fiscal year and our plans for next year when I make the statement I promised to make in the house when I bring down my supplementary financial measures.

subsubtopic: CYPRUS-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON PRESENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs regarding the situation in Cyprus. I would ask the minister whether he can acquaint the house with the terms and conditions under which a settlement is being sought in that area and what response has been received from the three governments most intimately affected, namely the governments of Greece, Turkey and Cyprus.

maintopic: RECOMMENDATIONS BY TAXATION COMMISSION RESPECTING DEPLETION ALLOWANCES
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: CYPRUS-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON PRESENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I indicated the other day, until final agreement has been reached I do not think it is possible to discuss the terms of the settlement. But it must

be evident that these include the position of forces on the island other than the forces supplied by the United Nations. The tension on the island has very considerably decreased. I continue to be hopeful for an early agreement in principle which will solve the immediate issue. This has to do with the withdrawal of forces other than those of the United Nations. However, there are at this moment certain problems which are still to be overcome at the United Nations and elsewhere to which the Secretary General a few moments ago advised me he is addressing himself in consultation with the countries concerned.
speakername: Hon. Paul  Marlin@Secretary of Stale for External Affairs

maintopic: RECOMMENDATIONS BY TAXATION COMMISSION RESPECTING DEPLETION ALLOWANCES
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: CYPRUS-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON PRESENT POSITION
speechtext: As a supplementary question, in view of the fact that some time this month the United Nations will be discussing the renewal of the mandate in Cyprus, is the Canadian government insisting that in such a renewed mandate the commander of the United Nations forces will have sufficient forces to police the situation and prevent the build-up of military forces in contravention of the terms of the Zurich agreement?

maintopic: RECOMMENDATIONS BY TAXATION COMMISSION RESPECTING DEPLETION ALLOWANCES
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: CYPRUS-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON PRESENT POSITION
speechtext: This will certainly be an aspect of the approach that we will be taking. I should point out to my hon. friend that the establishment of a United Nations force is something that depends not only on the action taken by the security council but on agreement made pursuant to the decision of the security council with the country on whose territory the force operates. I can assure my hon. friend that this question is very much in our minds.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to put a question to the Minister of Justice.
In view of the fact that he has stated several times that he would introduce a comprehensive bill to amend the Criminal Code, particularly as far as divorce and possibly abortion are concerned, could he inform the house whether he intends to introduce separate bills on divorce and on abortion so as to enable each member to express his opinions freely on these important questions.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DIVORCE AND ABORTION

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Thursday, November 30, consideration of the motion of Miss LaMarsh for the second reading of Bill
Administration of all National Museums No. S-2, to establish a corporation for the administration of the national museums of Canada.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CORPORATION FOR ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last evening I mentioned there was a totem pole restoration program in existence in British Columbia, and I thought it might be an appropriate opportunity for the federal government, through the corporation or through one of the museums under federal government authority, to participate in that restoration program and in effect establish a sort of museum on site, the site being the location of the original totems of various tribes on the west coast.
The contribution made to art by the west coast tribes has been tremendous and prolific. Unfortunately a great many of the works of art of the people of the west coast have found their way into collections and museums in other parts of the world. In fact I heard that a few years ago the national museum spent some $40,000, though I am not quite certain this is the exact figure, to purchase a collection of masks and other carvings which were the property of Lord Blossom.
This year the Vancouver Art Gallery exhibited a collection of works of art of the west coast tribes as a centennial project. It is as beautiful a collection as I have ever seen assembled in Canada. However, in order to assemble the works for this particular showing it was necessary for those who contributed to it, and particularly for Bill Reid who is an artist of high quality especially in gold and silver carvings, to travel quite extensively to museums in the United States in order to ask permission to get back for the purpose of that particular showing some of the works that these museums had lent. As I said, I think it was one of the finest collections that has ever been seen in Canada.
The works of a very prolific and highly gifted artist of the Haida people, Charles Edenshaw, were also there. They were indescribably beautiful carvings in black and red on silver, bone and wood. I was there the day the late Charles Edenshaw's daughter, Mrs. Emily White-a grand, elderly lady now-came down from Grimshaw to see the works of her father assembled and on display. Everyone who went through the art gallery in Vancouver this year was amazed at the beauty of the totem collection there.
The point I have been trying to make is that on many occasions in the past not too
4932	COMMONS
Administration of all National Museums great an interest has been shown in preserving or retaining the works of art of the west coast Indian tribes, and as a consequence they have found their way into other hands and into other collections and museums all over the world. Perhaps there will be no further opportunity to collect the materials and the works of art of the past because most of them have either been placed in museums, have been allowed to rot on the site, or have been lost.
However, in the last couple of years a group of anthropologists and archaeologists working under the national museum have visited certain areas on the west coast together with some officials of the provincial government, to search through and dig amongst the sites of the villages which existed in those areas in the past in an attempt to discover in greater detail some of the history of our native tribes. I think this might be a function of the museums which could be expanded.
There are a few provisions in the bill before us on which I would like some clarification. First of all I should like to know whether it will be permissible under the act for the museums to loan their works of art to local community museums or to provincial museums. I should also like to ask whether provision would be made under the bill for travelling exhibits. Both these measures would meet with approval because, particularly in this centennial year, increased interest has been shown in the establishment of museums as centennial projects.
A number of these have been opened in my area, and a couple of them which were previously in existence have concentrated to a large degree upon the collection and display of native Indian art objects. I think it would be of tremendous value if in addition to any of the collections and exhibits they now have, they could borrow from time to time some particularly fine works of art to display to the people who visit these areas and who may not have an opportunity to visit any of the national museums or see any of the travelling exhibits.
There is a provision in the bill which states that the Surplus Crown Assets Act shall not apply to the corporation. I assume this means it will not be possible for the museums to declare as surplus any of the exhibits they have, and thus they will not be able to dispose of them through the Crown Assets Disposal Corporation. If my impression is correct I think this is a commendable feature of the bill.

I rise, Mr. Speaker, to say a few words in support of the plea of the hon. member for Carleton that this bill go to committee. I know the minister has already declined this request, but I feel it would have been useful to hear from the directors presently involved in the administration of the several museums this bill seeks to incorporate, and to have their very learned reaction to the principle of the bill. As you know, Mr. Speaker, we are not able to call upon this expertise when we are dealing with a measure in the house. It was the late John F. Kennedy who said that of those to whom much is given, much is required. In our time, not only in our centennial year but within our time in history, a great deal has been given to our people. There has been an accumulation of a great deal of history in the arts and sciences that is well worth preserving.
Though in our centennial year we have not been able to achieve the establishment of a national museum building, which I am sure all members deplore along with the minister, I am confident that in the not too distant future there will be a fine museum which will be a credit to our country. I am worried, however, that when the high court of history sits in judgment on us with regard to the way in which during our brief span of history we have fulfilled our responsibilities to the nation, this measure may not be regarded as fulfilling those responsibilities for building and housing in a museum those things that need to be preserved.
After all, in our short span of existence as a country we have seen the change from the
December 1, 1967
COMMONS DEBATES	4933
horse and buggy to the automobile, and then to travel in the space age. We have seen the disappearance of steam power, the development of electrical energy and now nuclear energy. We have witnessed wave after wave of immigration which has added to the multicultural basis of our nation about which we like to boast. We have seen the slow flowering of the arts and sciences, and witnessed the halting advance of democracy in social concerns.
Somewhere these developments should be adequately recorded so that future generations may come to see them. I am just wondering whether the manner in which we are dealing with this very important question, namely by incorporating these museums under one crown corporation, will achieve those things we desire to achieve through this bill. My question simply is, would the minister reconsider the request to send this measure to a committee?

Mr. Speaker, like the previous speakers I shall try to be brief in my remarks on this bill. I support the plea the hon. member for Carleton made last night. I thought his point was well taken. I support it, not because the other place may not have reviewed this matter in sufficient depth but because there are areas of concern in the broad concept of this bill that ought to be properly aired. We ought to do something to make our great paintings, sculptures and other works of art more readily available to all our people. For that reason I join with the hon. member for Carleton and others who have urged the minister to refer this bill to a committee of this house, or to a joint committee, for further consideration.
December 1, 1967
4934	COMMONS
Administration of all National Museums
Mainly I want to say this. I shall propose an amendment to the bill. Though it is a slight amendment it will, if adopted, enable our youth to benefit more than they now benefit from the art objects we have collected and that we shall collect as the years go by. Our universities at the present time are embarked on the greatest expansion in our country's history. That expansion has not yet ended. Our universities are erecting wonderful, fireproof, air conditioned and sprinkler protected buildings, and perhaps we are missing a good bet by not using these buildings for art shows.
That has been proposed but not spelled out in detail. The clause that gives the corporation authority to sponsor and assist travelling shows is good, but vague. I should like the bill to say specifically that the major universities of our country may be regarded as museums of Canada. Perhaps that provision might be narrowed to refer to the libraries that are being built on our campuses.
Hon. members may have noticed that in the last three or four years wonderful new libraries have been built on our campuses, and these libraries have ample space at their entrances to accommodate art shows. The buildings are fireproof, and almost always security guards are present. If we want our young people to be exposed to art I suggest that by using the libraries on campuses for art shows we could bring about that result.
A major obstacle in the past to such art shows has been cost. Most universities from time to time hold an art show, usually somebody's collection, but most universities have not had the money to keep changing their art shows. As I say, most of them have neither the finances nor an adequate security staff for this. Perhaps if there were precise authority for this in the bill our major universities might have revolving art shows; the shows might be changed every six months, say, or once a year, and our undergraduates passing through university would have an opportunity to be exposed once or twice a year, throughout their university careers, to many art treasures. Throughout a university career an undergraduate might see 200 or 300 art treasures. The universities have the space for these shows, and that space is not being used except occasionally.
Unless our young people go out of their way in places like Ottawa to see art treasures, or unless they see the odd travelling art show, they have little opportunity to be exposed to our culture. They do not see what Canadian talent has produced in the past or


what the talented artists of this world have produced over the last 1,000 years. That is wrong. Understandably in the past, because libraries in universities were not fireproof or as well protected as they are today, the authorities in Ottawa felt reluctant about letting art treasures leave the vaults of Ottawa. Now, with more modern buildings on our campuses, buildings that are well protected against fire and other risks, perhaps consideration might be given to releasing art treasures to be shown in them. I commend that course of action to the minister. I should like to see in this country the best art museums in the world. I hope the minister will give consideration to my suggestion and incorporate the appropriate wording in the bill.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to the minister last evening, and I agree with many of her remarks. She said we were experiencing a renaissance in the field of museums and art galleries in Canada. I agree with that. I am sure that all across this country federal participation in centennial projects, especially projects under which art galleries and museums have been erected, has been appreciated. That participation has been a factor in the renaissance. I congratulate the national gallery and its director, through the minister, for the two outstanding centennial exhibitions.

The 300 years of Canadian art exhibition in itself was an education for any Canadians seeing it. Equally good is the present exhibition, which blends Canadian history and artistic development. I commend it to any member who has not been to the gallery to see it.
[DOT] (12 noon)
At the same time, Mr. Speaker, I cannot quite understand the provision in the bill that places all the museums and the national gallery in the charge of one over-all organization. The minister stated last night that this move would save money. I doubt that very much. If any change is to be made in relation to art or the national gallery or the museum, then saving money should be the last consideration. If we wanted to save money at the expense of a very important area of our national development then we would not have a gallery, and we would likely not have some of the museums either. The gallery will cost money, and I anticipate that if we want to continue our development
December I, 1S67

it will cost us even more money. The problem is really one of education and enthusiastic salesmanship to justify a most important expenditure in the development of the country.
I was wandering whether the minister was not overly impressed by the United States pavilion at Expo, which managed to combine in a very light-hearted fashion the most recent developments in science along with some of the most recent, if startling, developments in art. The problem is that we are moving into an era of austerity, the end of which is not yet in sight. It is an era of austerity of which we were fully reminded last night when we listened to the Minister of Finance presenting his budget to the house.
I suggest that if the visitors from the United States to the U.S. pavilion at Expo had been polled on their view as to which exhibits in time of austerity should be cut out, as between the scientific displays and the displays of modern art, there would be no doubt in anybody's mind what the answer would be and which exhibits in the pavilion would first fall victim to any austerity drive.
The hon. member for Rosthern raised a most important point, but I would not for a moment agree with what he said. I would not accept the hon. member for Rosthern as an art critic for a single minute. However, he did point out that when it comes to art there is a great divergence of opinion. We do accept the possibility of there being bad art. However, we do not accept the possibility of bad science; there is no such thing at the moment. All scientific endeavour as such is sacred and good and we can justify almost any expense if it is based on scientific advance.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, when one reads the bill and finds that the credit balances in the national gallery purchase account are going to be moved over to the national museum's purchase account, one wonders how the division is going to be made between the conflicting demands of art through the gallery and those of science through the science museum or the museum of natural history or any of the projected museums of the future. Certainly great expenditure will be required over the next few years to construct several new national museums. However, as I say, how do you arbitrate the conflicting claims of the national gallery and the national museum? It may be that the minister would like the budget of the national gallery to be buried in the budget for science and for
Administration of all National Museums museums so the public could no longer distinguish between the funds allocated to one or the other.
I hope this is not going to be the case, Mr. Speaker, and that such a step would be considered a sort of doctrine of despair. Surely we in Canada can develop an appreciation of art and its place in society. I hope the national gallery will be allowed to exist as a separate entity and to have a separate budget. I hope its value will be fully appreciated, and in the long run I feel this would be the better course.
I do not think the minister gave us sufficient explanation last evening of the thinking that prompts the change proposed by this bill. Other hon. members have pointed out the dangers that are there, and I hope that before the bill is passed the minister will give a further explanation, or that the bill will be referred to a committee. In the latter case we could hear from the director of the national gallery and learn whether she is fully satisfied that this measure will not constrict the developement of that most important part of our culture.

Mr. Speaker, this is the type of bill which I think should not go through the house in iust five or ten minutes but on the other hand it should not be very much delayed. The only reason I am speaking on it is a certain experience I had 20 years ago when, as a new and rather brash member of the Manitoba legislature, I drew to the attention of that august assembly the importance of the museum which is situated in the city of Winnipeg. This had satisfactory results. It stirred up interest on the part of the provincial legislators and encouraged those people who were dedicating their efforts to the advancement of the museum.
Similarly now, I do not think it is a bad thing for parliament to indicate that its members have a real interest in the museums of our country and in our national art gallery. We can hastily pass legislation without comment, but if we do that with this legislation those who work in the museums and art gallery cannot be certain whether it is due to a careless indifference on the part of members or whether parliament has an active interest which it has not expressed. By speaking today I would like to display my active interest in our art gallery and museums, as the minister displayed her interest last night. Parliament as a whole, representing the people of this country, will show that interest by our recording in Hansard our appreciation of the work of those who have been operating and maintaining our museums and of those who have supported this effort. Over the last 20 years I have seen a great upsurge of interest in the history and records of this country as portrayed in our museums. This is all to the good. It is one of the means by which we establish our Canadian identity.
I was quite impressed with the minister's remarks last night. Her interest in these fields is intense. I was also impressed with

DEBATES	December 1, 1967
the remarks of my very learned and distinguished colleague from Carleton, who drew attention to the exciting history of Canada, a history which I fully agree is exciting. The more we bring it to the attention of our young people the better it will be for Canada as a whole. This has happened during the last few years, and particularly during centennial year. One of the finest things to emerge from centennial year is the interest across Canada, in small places and in large, in Canada's wonderful history.
I recall my own keen interest as a student and young man in museums. I recall my first visit to the great city of Toronto many years ago. The first place I visited there was the museum. I was more than impressed and my knowledge of the world was enlarged by the exhibitions there. I have always had an interest in these matters and I express that interest today.
With regard to the bill I entertain some doubts that this is the best method of going about the work of the art gallery and the museums. As members have said, there is a sharp difference between an art gallery and a museum. A museum shows things from the past and the record of past events. It displays scientific and archaeological records. An art gallery has a different approach and a different appeal.
I am one of those who can appreciate a painting by Constable, but for the life of me I cannot understand some of the modem art which is placed before my eyes. So I cannot be a judge. I do not feel I am capable of making a judgment with regard to art other than that I like something and dislike something else.
I think that bringing the art gallery and the museums under the terms of one bill may be a mistake. If it is being done just for financial reasons then I think members were justified in asking for the bill to be referred to a committee prior to passage in order to determine whether or not this is wise. However, 1 understand the minister prefers not to do that. Consequently we will have to get on with the bill and hope for the best in the future. In any event these reservations have now been placed before the house.
I think that the general attention to our art galleries and museums is good. As I say, it is right that parliament should pay some attention to them. It is right that we should vote money for these purposes. All we can hope for is that their administration will be effective so that the people of Canada at large
December 1, 1987

will benefit from these marks of an advanced civilization. It is only the higher civilizations that maintain such records of their histories and traditions. I conclude by saying that I support the bill, with the reservations that have been expressed so clearly by my colleague from Carleton.

Mr. Speaker, I want to say a few brief words on the bill. First of all, I congratulate the minister for introducing it. I think that over all it is good legislation. However, there are one or two points about it which disturb me to some extent. The first concerns clause 13(b) which calls for the establishment of advisory committees consisting of members of the board or persons other than members or both. If permission is to be granted for the establishing of advisory committees, I would prefer that the appointees be separate from the board. I do not like the idea of mixing the two functions.
I recommend to the minister that the appropriate form should be as enacted in section 14 of the act to provide for the establishment of a Canadian Film Development Corporation, passed by this house in February, 1967. That section reads as follows:
The minister may, on the recommendation of the corporation, appoint an advisory group broadly representative of the professional associations, exhibitors, distributors and unions in the Canadian film industry and including other qualified persons, to advise the corporation on matters which the minister or the corporation may refer to it.
I would suggest that this is a better example of how to go about forming advisory committees.
The other point I wish to bring to the attention of the house is that this bill was the cause of the resignation of the director of the human history section of the national museum, Dr. Richard Glover. I wish to quote briefly from Dr. Glover's statement, published in the Ottawa Journal of April 24, 1967. This is part of what he said:
-the act does not give directors complete charge of the professional business of their museums. Instead, it leaves a new and as yet unappointed board of trustees to make by-laws prescribing what each museum director's authority shall be: and the directors will be able to do only those things which the trustees may see fit to assign to them. All business not so assigned is given to a new officer called a secretary-general. Here the act falls sadly short of the government's professed purpose.
Worse follows. Another clause empowers the board of trustees to appoint consultative committees, which are to be composed "of professional people to advise it," as the Senate was told. I acknowledge that committees may from time to
Administration of all National Museums time make useful recommendations on broad general policy; and that directors themselves may sometime welcome the help of advisory committees of their own. But these consultative committees of professional people reporting to the board on professional matters are quite another tiling.
[DOT] (12:20 p.m.)
The meaning of this clause, as explained by the government's spokesman in the Senate, is that the trustees may expect professional advice on the museums' programs from two different sources- their consultative committees on the one hand and the museum's own experienced and highly professional staff on the other. But advice from two different sources often differs and the prospects of conflict, friction and unrest which this clause opens up are as obvious as they are deplorable.
When a person of the stature of Dr. Glover resigns on grounds of principle involving what I just read and in addition the fact that the government has cut back on the construction of new museum buildings, I think the matter should be gone into a little more carefully. I do not believe his protestations should be dismissed without some consideration having been given to them. I recognize that there are problems in this regard but I should like to suggest to the minister that this bill be referred to a committee after second reading in order that we may go into some of these aspects.

speechtext:
All the directors have recently been appointed. Dr. Boggs is the director of the National Gallery. I believe she has brought a really new spirit of excitement to the gallery and to its work. She was appointed within the past two years. Dr. Ban-field was appointed in February, 1964. Dr. Taylor was appointed this year and Dr. Baird was appointed in October, 1966. All these people are young, vigorous and interested in their work. They are highly qualified specialists. The interesting thing is that these people are civil servants. They are appointed under that act and are not at the moment in the capacity of some of our appointees as public servants. That has been one of the criticisms often made of the situation in the past. Of course, it leads to a problem when one is looking for the very best persons to appoint to the various directorships.
I believe Canada can rejoice in the fact that, as it so happened, within a year or so before centennial year these exciting and vigorous young personalities were taken on as directors of our national museums. Indeed they are national museums. If hon. members will look at the terms of the bill and think for a moment of museums as they know them, such as the museum of natural history, the museum of natural science and a museum which now is included along with the others, the new air museum, and then look at them from the point of view of what we understand as a classical art gallery, they will find that the words apply in each case and that while many people think of the galleries as being separate they are in fact not. As a matter of fact the association of directors of galleries is known as the association of museum directors. As you know, some

DEBATES	December 1, 1987
of the great museums of the world, including the one in Montreal, are known as museums of art and not galleries of art. This is because they are in fact collections of treasures.
It may cost the better part of $1 million to collect a treasure for the art museum and perhaps only $10,000 to collect an old railway car for the science museum. Yet some of the exhibits in the science museum are unique, irreplaceable and without any limit to their value. I think the concern of people who are particularly interested in one or the other of the museums, including the galleries, is that if you put them all together and have one general account either the science people, the art gallery people or somebody else will get more money. This has been very prominent concern of the directors as well. However, in each case the directors will run their institution and will prepare their budgets every year. These will be put together as a whole budget and the money parliament votes will be distributed in the amounts budgeted for. While this is something which should be watched it has not been contemplated, nor should members be concerned, that the directors will not be very alert to the fact that their portion of the money in the non-lapsing fund is there for their expenditure.
I should like particularly to thank the hon. member for Skeena for telling the chamber about the reconstruction of the west coast Haida totems and for his very interesting suggestion of making an on site museum. I had not appreciated that this was taking place in some parts of British Columbia. Indeed, I had thought that perhaps the only permanent record we would have of totems in their place would be the paintings of Emily Carr. Certainly this is a most interesting thought which I will be happy to pass on to the appropriate officials and even the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development which is responsible for historic sites. I had never heard of any other place in North America where there still are totems in their original position which can be restored and viewed. I think that this is a national heritage which we should have for a long time in the future.
I should like also to comment on the "Arts of the Raven" show which was mentioned. My own personal opinion, for what it is worth, is that this is one of the most superb shows I have ever seen. Anyone who missed it in Vancouver this year in its four or five month run really missed a Canadian show
December 1, 1967

which cannot ever be replaced. As hon. members will realize, when we talk about travelling exhibits and sending out national treasures more and more, whether they relate to libraries or new cultural centres, it should be remembered that there is always a toll on the treasures as a result of the travelling. We were told in respect of the "Arts of the Raven" show that this is the last time any of these treasures will ever be lent for exhibition because of the fact that, unavoidably, the treasures become damaged in travelling. I think the national gallery and the museums have long been devotees of travelling exhibits and assistance to other museums. As you will see in the bill, there is provision for that to continue.
[DOT] (12:30 p.m.)
The hon. member for Rosthern suggested that there has been a decline in values and that we should only purchase things of value. No one could agree with him more in that regard than I, but that does not mean that we cannot buy contemporary works for both the museum and the gallery. These items were used by them in former times for the purpose of their potlatch celebrations.
The minister is probably aware that at one time the parliament of Canada took action to outlaw these festivals so far as the Indian people on the west coast were concerned. As part of the business of enforcing the law the government of Canada took into its possession a very large number of the beautiful items which had been part of the regalia of the potlatch festivals. I understand that these items are still in the possession of the government of Canada and in the custody of the national museum in particular.
At a considerably later point in time parliament saw fit to remove from the Indian Act that section of the law which forbade potlatching. In other words, it is quite legal now for the Indian peoples on the west coast to hold these festivals should they so desire. I think I should say at once that it is most unlikely they would be revived fully in the manner and to the extent they once existed; nevertheless there is that tradition of festivals.

speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. S-3, respecting the armed forces of countries visiting Canada.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the basic purpose of this bill is to repeal the Visiting Forces (North Atlantic Treaty Organization) Act, the Visiting Forces (British Commonwealth) Act, and the Visiting Forces (United States of America) Act, and to replace them with one act which would provide for the rights, privileges and duties of the armed forces of any other nation when visiting in Canada. The Visiting Forces (British Commonwealth) Act was enacted in 1932 as a result of the Statute of Westminster. It provides for the privileges, immunities and duties of visiting forces from other parts of the commonwealth when in Canada. Reciprocal legislation was enacted by nations of the commonwealth to provide for Canadian forces visiting those countries.

During the second world war, with many United States forces visiting Canada their position was provided for by an order in council under the War Measures Act. When at the conclusion of the war it became apparent that United States forces would continue to visit Canada from time to time, the Visiting Forces (United States of America) Act was enacted. There is no reciprocal United States legislation as under the law of that country a visiting force automatically carries with it the right to hold courts martial, administer discipline, and so on.
In 1949 Canada became a member of NATO. One of the agreements entered into at the time by Canada was the agreement between the parties to the North Atlantic Treaty regarding the status of their forces. This agreement provided for the status, privileges and duties of the armed forces of one NATO country when in another NATO country.
Canadian legislation was required to approve and implement this agreement. The legislation known as the Visiting Forces (North Atlantic Treaty Organization) Act was enacted for that purpose in 1951. At the time this act was drafted it was foreseen that the armed forces of non-NATO states might visit Canada from time to time and that provision should be made for the status of such forces in Canada. This was done by providing in the act that forces of non-NATO countries could be brought under the act by the governor in council, designating the countries from which they came as associated states under section 5.
Since the visting forces of NATO act was passed, armed forces of many non-NATO countries, particularly the emerging African states, have visited Canada for training and other purposes. It is therefore felt that it is not appropriate that the forces of these non-NATO countries should have their status in Canada determined by an act of parliament designed to implement the north Atlantic treaty. The government therefore decided that it would submit to parliament for approval a bill repealing all the existing visiting forces acts and providing for visiting forces in a uniform way. I may say that this is the course that has been followed by the United Kingdom and most other NATO countries requiring such legislation.

It would seem to me that argument could be turned around and used against anyone who thinks it has validity. I suggest to hon. members that if young people from the early teenage years who now have access to so many facets of society are not responsible, and therefore should not be given the opportunity to vote, we must be very fearful of that situation. It has always seemed to me that real enlightenment does not come until people become responsible, and that the sometimes erratic judgments people make of issues that are raised, and the opinions that they hold, are very largely the result of a lack of responsibility and a lack of participation. From time to time one hears suggestions and criticisms by newspapers and others about the lack of responsibility amongst members of this house. I think it would be interesting if we could allow the various editors and publishers of newspapers across the country the opportunity to sit in the house, and to function as living, breathing members of parliament for a period sufficiently lengthy to enable them to gain enlightenment about the responsibility resting upon a member of parliament in this place.
It seems to me, if one could use that analogy, the same thing has to happen if we are going to obtain more responsible democracy. We must allow more and more young people to participate early in the democratic processes. We have come to the conclusion somehow that there is really only one way in which people participate in the democratic process, and that is by going to the polling booth on election day to cast a ballot. We have deluded ourselves, Mr. Speaker, if we think that is the only aspect of participation that is really important. Anyone who has studied the history of civilizations knows that very often some of the most important things that happen to a society bear no relationship to the actual, recognized function of choosing or not choosing governments and representatives. If we are afraid to entrust young men and young women at the age of 18 with the exercise of responsibility at the ballot box, then we should be very fearful indeed of the great influence these people are already having on many of our social structures today.
I say to you, sir, it is inconsistent for us to establish the Company of Young Canadians or to send young people all over the world as representatives of either state organizations or

church organizations, and then at this juncture say to them that this is where their responsibility ends. This kind of inconsistency, I am sure, flys in the face of many young people, and to which they can only reply, "Sham".
I do not plan to take up a great deal of time this evening because I am hopeful that we can either conclude the debate in this hour and have the bill passed-I am sure hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) will agree with that-or else save the precious time in private members hour that might be spent in discussing this measure by referring it to the committee on privi-liges and elections. If that is impossible because the committee has not been constituted, perhaps we could have some real commitment from a representative of the government toward this end. I believe it is the wish of members on every side of this house that we take action now in this parliament, so the next time a federal election is called all adults beyond the age of 18 will participate fully in that election.
I should like to quote a speech made by one member of this house on July 14, 1960, as reported at page 6277 of Hansard:
There is a great deal to be said in the circumstances of today for the reduction of the voting age from 21 to 18, and most of the major arguments in favour of such a change were given by the hon. member for Assiniboia. The argument which I think must make the greatest appeal is that we do not hesitate as a state to call on young people to fight for our country and, if necessary to die for our country, as thousands under the age of 21 have done. We ask them to accept the supreme obligation of citizenship in this regard, irrespective of whether they are 21 or 20 or 19 or 18, so it seems to me that if we ask Canadians to take on that obligation the time has come when they should have the privilege of voting so they may do their share in determining the policies which might affect the situations in which they would be asked to share in this supreme obligation.
I agree with the words of the hon. member.

Mr. Speaker, I have no hesitation in entering this debate, because this is the first occasion on which an opportunity has presented itself for me to express my views on a subject which is of more than academic interest to many in Canada.
I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Prince (Mr. MacDonald), the mover of this bill which is to amend the Canada Elections Act and lower the voting age from 21 to 18. That is a worthy objective, more especially since the hon. member himself is one of the younger members in the house. I extend to him my congratulations and good wishes. This bill is timely. I have reason to believe that this matter will be under active consideration by the government, if not during the present session, then certainly early in the new year. In any event, I am all for the principle of the bill.
One would have to take into consideration whether the 18-year-old is really interested in voting. Much to my disappointment-and no doubt the hon. member was disappointed -during the recent Ontario provincial elections qualified students at Lakehead University failed to be really interested in the elections, and only 27 per cent of those eligible turned out to vote. Similar experiences were found in other Ontario universities, and this brings the question of whether it is really
Canada Elections Act
worth while extending the franchise to include boys and girls of 18 years of age.
One explanation for the apparent lack of interest of university students in the issues of the Ontario provincial elections was that some students did not know about transfer arrangements, in spite of the wide publicity and appeals made on the campuses to register. For example, it was reported that at Glendon college, Toronto, the returning officer reported that special enumerators sat nearly all day in a room on the Glendon campus, and that of an estimated 60 eligible students, exactly 12 registered, or 20 per cent of those who could have qualified.
I am told that some student leaders suggested that the lack of interest was due to a dull campaign which focussed on uninteresting matters, including the future of Canada as a united country, and the crisis in housing. Why did not the probing students, who usually are very vocal on any and all political issues, ask questions about matters they care about?
One of our metropolitan dailies, in an interesting observation, reported that the oft reported leftist tendencies of university students led some to believe that the majority of students would vote for the New Democratic party candidates. On nearly all campuses in the province of Ontario the N.D.P. candidate ran third.
On the other hand, I believe that in the majority of cases an 18-year-old can be sufficiently responsible to express an intelligent opinion by means of the ballot box. In an election, every adult has one vote; as everyone knows, he has a direct influence on the outcome equal to that of every other elector. Degree of interest and intelligence are not taken into consideration. Such a system assumes the exercise of the suffrage by every qualified citizen; that is, it assumes the total involvement of the population in self government. Hence, voting entails a considerable responsibility as well as a privilege.
The franchise should theoretically be granted to every citizen. In practice, however, the application of this principle is not feasible. Obviously babes in arms are not capable of voting in an intelligent or responsible manner. The purpose of imposing qualifications on suffrage, then, is to limit to mature citizens participation in the collective decision. But, one may ask, who are "mature citizens"? Is there an examination which proves maturity? If so, is anyone capable of administering it? In the absence of both we have accepted the need for establishing some

December 1, 1967
Canada Elections Act
indisputable criteria which are related to mature judgment.
Age is beyond dispute and, to a degree, is correlated with maturity. So despite such objections as the fact that different people mature at different rates, and that there is little difference in an individual's maturity between his twentieth and twenty first year, the arbitrary age criterion has been accepted as necessary for practical considerations.
The next logical question is as to the age at which suffrage should be granted. The lack of consensus on this matter is evident in the fact that of the ten provinces of Canada, four-Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Ontario and Manitoba-have adopted 21 as the voting age; the three provinces of, Newfoundland, Alberta and British Columbia have adopted 19 years, and the three provinces of, Prince Edward Island, Quebec and Saskatchewan have adopted 18 years. The federal voting age is currently 21 years.
Hon. E. C. Manning, premier of Alberta for the past 27 years, has this to say of young people:
The younger generation of Canadians is capable of political thought and action at a level of maturity much higher than that characterizing party politics in this country at the present time. Youth today is quick to detect, and is strongly repulsed by sham and superficiality. Young people who are looking for purpose, conviction, inspiration, and leadership in matters of private and national concern will not, nor should be expected to, be satisfied by gimmicks and slogans, cliches and promises, and slick but shallow promotional campaigns. There will be little room in the Canada of tomorrow for elections without issues, politicians without philosophical standards, parties without relevant policies, or citizenship without definition and purpose.
I feel that the lowering of the voting age should be accompanied by a program to increase political education. What is at present being taught in our high schools about civic responsibilties is not adequate, and I would suggest a course in citizenship and politics to give students greater knowledge of their responsibilities.

When considering amendments to and revisions in the Canada Elections Act, to eliminate discrepancies and discrimination in our present regulations, the necessary provision for patients confined to hospitals to cast their votes in a federal general election is of primary importance.
An active general hospital presents a problem. Very few patients are in hospital as long as six weeks, in which event it would become necessary both to enumerate them and to

have them vote in a hospital poll. Of the few who are, it is usually impossible to predict which ones will be in hospital on election day, and therefore as far as I know none were enumerated in the last several elections. Some did remain in hospital through the enumeration and into the election period, and were therefore disfranchised. They may have been enumerated at their homes, and would have voted at their home polls if it had been physically possible. I presume the spouse at home might well have included the one in hospital in the residential enumeration. Most other patients were at home at enumeration time, but were admitted to hospital later. Neither group can vote in the hospital, although a poll is set up there to handle the few student nurses and other personnel living in hospital residences. The exception to this is the candidate's right to appoint two agents to vote in the poll and to represent him there.
There has been talk of a permanent voters' registry for all people. This would solve the problem, but it will likely take a long time and may be impossible. It is not an excuse for delaying action to protect the franchises of several specific groups. This measure can deal with hospital patients; other measures should be introduced to deal with university students, especially if the trimester system of university education becomes widespread.
It should be relatively easy to establish a solution for patients living in the same riding in which they are hospitalized. A simple method that occurs to me would be for the returning officer to contact the other poll by phone, and satisfy himself that this particular person was entitled to a vote. However this is not good enough to ensure against fraud and illegal voting.
Someone would have to obtain a slip from the district returning officer in the person's original poll. This could be delivered to the hospital in-patient, who would then present it to the district returning officer in a poll located in or adajcent to the hospital. One assumes he would be physically able to travel inside the hospital to the polling booth. A good number, perhaps 50 per cent are able to do so.
For those living in Fort William, for example, and then requiring hospitalization in a university centre such as Toronto or Winnipeg, the difficulties are rather formidable. The same system could be used; but the patient might find it more difficult to be sure which candidate was the better one, or the best one. It would also require making an
December 1, 1967

application several days prior to election day, to allow for transmission of the slip from one district returning officer to another, via the patient. For those who might be living in the same city, but residing in one riding and staying in a hospital in another riding, the difficulties would fall somewhere between the situation I have already described. If a patient's relative, friend, or agent presented a request to grant the patient the right to vote in another poll, then the advance poll district returning officer could strike the name oil the original poll list and issue a slip to this effect for transmission to the patient. The patient could then present the slip on election day to the district returning officer at the hospital poll.
I realize that this is not the object of the bill under discussion. Nevertheless I think that when considering any changes to the elections act these should include measures which will ensure voting facilities for every qualified voter, whether he is at home or temporarily in a health institution away from home.
To conclude, Mr. Speaker, I want to say unequivocally that I am in favour of the purposes of this bill, and if and when it comes to a vote I will certainly vote for it.
